layer.description: Overlay multiple marks in the same coordinate system
layer.usage: Use 'layer' array with multiple spec objects
characteristics: All layers share the same space
Marks are drawn on top of each other
Visual overlay only - no structural hierarchy
layer.data_transformation: No transformation - each layer uses same or different data
when_to_use: Overlaying multiple series with different visual encodings

examples.description: Overlay points on a line to show both trend and individual values
examples.structure: layer: [line mark, point mark] - both use same x/y scales

examples.description: Show bars for individual values with a horizontal line indicating mean
examples.structure: layer: [bar mark, rule mark] - rule shows aggregate statistic

examples.description: Points with statistical overlay showing distribution
examples.structure: layer: [point mark, area mark] - area computed from point data

facet.description: Create small multiples by splitting data into subsets
facet.usage: Use 'facet' to define the faceting field(s), then use 'each column', 'each row', or 'each grid' to specify the visualization for each facet
characteristics: Each facet is an independent visualization
Each facet has its own scales
Data is logically grouped by facet field
All facets use the same mark and encoding structure
when_to_use: Showing same visualization for different groups
Reducing visual clutter from overlapping data

examples.description: Show time series for each region in separate panels
examples.structure: facet by 'region' → each column shows line chart for one region
facet by 'category' → each row shows histogram for one category

examples.description: Scatter plots across two categorical dimensions
examples.structure: facet by 'year' and 'country' → grid layout with scatter plot in each cell

examples.description: Compare two groups with mirrored facets for symmetrical comparison
examples.structure: facet by 'gender' with x-axis mirroring → male on left, female on right (mirrored horizontally)
examples.note: Can mirror on x-axis or y-axis depending on layout orientation

fields.field2: Optional second field for grid layout

facet_wrappers.each grid: Facets arranged in 2D grid (requires field + field2)

concat.description: Arrange different views together without data transformation
concat.usage: Use 'concat' object with 'layout' field, then use 'same row', 'same column', or 'spec' array to specify the views
characteristics: No data transformation - each view maintains original structure
Views can use shared or independent datasets
Each view can have different mark types and encodings
concat.data_transformation: No transformation - each view uses its own data
when_to_use: Showing different visualizations side by side

examples.description: Bar chart showing totals next to table showing details
examples.structure: concat: {layout: 'same row'} → [bar chart, table] - different mark types

examples.description: Line chart for revenue above bar chart for units sold
examples.structure: concat: {layout: 'same column'} → [line chart, bar chart] - shared x-axis via resolve
concat: {layout: 'crossing'} → scatter at center, histograms on margins

layouts.crossing: Views positioned at different locations with optional shared axes

nested.description: Embed child visualizations within parent marks
characteristics: Child visualizations are embedded inside parent marks
Parent mark must have a valid canvas (not N/A)
Child size is constrained by parent size when canvas is 'inner'
Each parent instance gets its own child visualization
Represents structural hierarchy, not just visual overlay
nested.data_transformation: struct[] → struct[][] (outer: parent elements, inner: child data for each parent)
when_to_use: Creating nested pie charts or donuts
Embedding small charts in scatter points
Each parent element needs its own independent child view

examples.description: Replace each tree node with a pie chart showing category breakdown
examples.structure: nested: {parent: tree mark, child: pie chart} - each node becomes a pie
examples.why_not_layer: Layer would overlay one pie on entire tree; nested creates one pie per node

examples.description: Each node in a network shows a bar chart of metrics
examples.structure: nested: {parent: graph mark, child: bar chart} - each node has its own bars
examples.why_not_layer: Layer cannot bind different data to each node position

examples.description: Outer ring contains inner rings for hierarchical data
examples.structure: nested: {parent: arc mark, child: arc mark} - structural parent-child relationship
examples.why_not_layer: Layer would just overlay arcs; nested respects hierarchy and sizing

examples.description: Each point in scatter contains a time series sparkline
examples.structure: nested: {parent: point mark, child: line chart} - each point gets its own trend
examples.why_not_layer: Layer would show one line for all points; nested shows one line per point

examples.description: Each geographic region contains a bar chart of local data
examples.structure: nested: {parent: geo mark, child: bar chart} - charts positioned within regions
examples.why_not_layer: Layer cannot position different charts inside different regions

nested_vs_layer.nested: Structural hierarchy - each parent gets its own child instance with different data
nested_vs_layer.layer: Visual overlay - marks share coordinate system, no parent-child data binding
nested_vs_layer.key_difference: Nested creates N child visualizations (one per parent), layer creates 1 overlay for all

child.canvas: Where child is drawn: 'inner' (inside parent) or 'top' (on top of parent)
